summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the French national framework. Rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law, marriage and legal gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, so the legal position a trans visitor faces in this region is the one that applies elsewhere in France.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. France has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area and being punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on roughly 40 referrals received since 2010. It found serious violations of fundamental rights persisting across all places of detention, including placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches, and recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 gender-recognition reform. Its recommendations also cover intersex and non-binary detainees.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a further opinion was necessary precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. The findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current through 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was raised before the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at an airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

The baseline for partner recognition dates from the marriage-equality law of 17 May 2013, which opened marriage to same-sex couples; international television coverage recorded France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect.

Within the region, the documented restriction concerns public assembly rather than trans status as such. The Côte-d'Or prefecture banned the Dijon Pride march from the city centre in June 2025, an event with over a decade of local history: pride marches have been organised in the Bourgogne cities of Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre since 2013, in the national context of marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994 to 1995 onward. The ban is an exception against the national legal baseline rather than the regional rule.
tangentialFactors:
France's national legal framework carries anti-discrimination protections covering LGBT people, and the national open-reference record states that these coexist with continued discrimination and violence, with reports of such incidents rising. The 2023 survey figure of 64% of trans people reporting identity-related discrimination indicates the scale of that gap between protection on paper and lived experience, and it applies to this region as to the rest of the country.

Two settings account for most of the documented trans-specific risk nationally: the prison system, where placement and isolation are improvised by each establishment, and the border, where identity-document checks have been carried out in view of other travellers. Neither risk is particular to Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, and no regional instrument modifies either.

The June 2025 restriction on the Dijon Pride march sits alongside a decade of uninterrupted organising in Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre, which shows regional public-assembly practice before and after the prefectural decision. It is best read as local administrative turbulence in a country where pride marches have multiplied since the mid-1990s.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté obtain legal gender recognition under the national procedure reformed in 2016, and that reform has not been shown by the CGLPL to have changed trans detainees' placement or treatment in custody. Residents held in the region's prisons are assigned on the same document-based basis as elsewhere in France, with no statutory rule and no consistent treatment between establishments.

Discrimination complaints are handled under the national anti-discrimination regime, and the Défenseur des droits has issued guidance directed at service providers who deal with trans people in their ordinary work. Residents who encounter refusals of service, employment discrimination or harassment in the region have access to the same national complaint machinery and to the associations whose testimony fed the ombuds's findings.

Regional residents organise Pride events in Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre, which have been held in Bourgogne since 2013. The June 2025 decision barring the Dijon march from the city centre is a prefectural public-order measure affecting assembly routes, and it does not alter the national legal rights of LGBT residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bourgogne-Franche-Comté-specific enforcement record for trans-related hate crime, no regional data on how the region's establishments place trans detainees, and no regional figures on document-marker issuance at prefectures in this region are sourced in the current inventory. Anything stated about the region's day-to-day practice rests on the national pattern.

The procedural history and any appeal or reinstatement of the June 2025 Dijon Pride march ban are not sourced, and the inventory does not indicate whether trans-specific objections were raised in the prefectural decision.

Whether the CGLPL's 2021 recommendations have been implemented in any specific establishment in this region remains unresolved in the sources consulted. The Défenseur des droits framework decision is cited by its content rather than by date in the inventory, so its exact issuance date is not established here.
